items.title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
items.excerpt: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey. Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history. But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming. Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

items.title: COP31 ends without climate pact as UN chief warns there is ‘no ambiguity in the science’ | UN News
items.excerpt: 22 November 2026 Climate and Environment COP31 ended on Sunday without a climate pact after negotiators failed to overcome divisions over fossil fuels, bringing two weeks of talks and two days of overtime to a close that UN Secretary-General António Guterres described as a “deeply disappointing” setback. Reacting to the collapse of COP31, the Secretary-General said he was “deeply disappointed” that governments meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, had failed to reach consensus, but stressed that the outcome did not alter the realities of the climate crisis. ### What you need to know - COP31 closed without a final climate pact after two weeks of negotiations and two days of overtime talks. - Disagreement over fossil fuel language proved the main obstacle to consensus. - Several countries formally objected to the final text, saying it weakened previous commitments and failed to meet the urgency of the climate crisis. - António Guterres called the outcome a setback but insisted there remains “no ambiguity in the science” and urged faster climate action. - Antalya has become the longest-running UN climate summit on record.

items.title: Politics chat: Lawmakers step up with only weeks to Democrats' control of Congress : NPR
items.excerpt: RASCOE: There is a funding deadline coming up on December 11. The president is demanding $350 billion in new defense spending. Funding deadlines and Congress always make people think about, is there going to be a shutdown? How likely is it that lawmakers don't come to an agreement in time? MCDANIEL: I mean, it's definitely possible that we see a government shutdown. I don't think we'll see 350 billion in new Pentagon spending, but I want to remind people that lawmakers are aware of the stakes here. Like you were pointing out, the federal government is the nation's largest employer, and we're coming off an election where the public just rebuked a Congress that dragged it through the longest shutdown in U.S. history. Some 90% of the public believes that the government is corrupt, that lawmakers advocate for their own self-interests rather than the public. They connect that back to a high cost of living. Plus, right now, Democrats are loath to fund the president's unpopular war in Iran, but they don't have full control until January. And so the calculus might be a short-term money for, you know, keeping their powder dry until the new year. RASCOE: And two outgoing Senate Republicans have also blocked Trump's nominees for various jobs. John Cornyn of Texas blocked an official from the Justice Department from a seat on a U.S. district court, and North Carolina's Thom Tillis blocked two nominees, one for a key U.S. cybersecurity agency and another to lead the Government Accountability Office. Tell us more about that last one. MCDANIEL: Yeah, the Government Accountability Office. This is a big deal. And in a lot of ways, the consequence is the president alienating so many lawmakers from his own party, right? Let's focus on the GAO. This accountability branch helps Congress with their oversight responsibilities. That's a key constitutional obligation they have. Trump and allies were trying to install a figure Democrats, and some Republicans, like you mentioned, viewed as too partisan. But the other issue for lawmakers was that it's another example of the White House and executive branch trying to yank control away from Congress, which has happened on everything from the power of the purse to the power to declare war. And I think in this environment, that power grab just wasn't going to fly. Still, it isn't as though Senate Republicans aren't going to do any confirmations, right? They will be laser-focused on confirming as many judges and other Cabinet - not Cabinet appointees - other presidential appointees, like ambassadors, before they lose their gavels in January. ... RASCOE: ...From Congress. Democrats are planning to launch any number of investigations once they take charge. On Friday, the president issued this new executive order that bars federal contractors from sharing information with Congress without instructions from the White House. Does this executive order have any teeth? MCDANIEL: Look, I'm not a lawyer. I'm not that smart. But I'll let them sort out the details. I do want to make one big point. The White House can do anything they want to try and prevent people from complying with the legal investigatory powers of Congress. But everyone, particularly if they're outside of government, is taking individual legal risk that the administration can't really insulate them from. That's legal bills. That's time. That's a potential contempt of Congress vote, reputational cost. And all of this is pretty high stakes, right? Getting dragged before Congress is no small thing. And remember what incoming House Oversight Committee chairman Robert Garcia, a Democrat, posted when Democrats had won the majority. He said, lawyer up. So his party and all of their investigatory committees aren't going to be timid at all at pursuing their legal avenues, no matter what executive orders the president issues.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries outlines healthcare areas where Democrats "can explore coming together" with Trump - CBS News
items.excerpt: Washington — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House speaker when his party takes control of Congress next year, outlined areas on Sunday where he said Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump. "Let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare," Jeffries said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." As Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate in the new year, following a slew of victories in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump expressed openness to working with Democrats in recent days — citing healthcare as a possible area for compromise. "I'm open to great healthcare," Mr. Trump said at a press briefing on Friday. "Now, can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans." Jeffries identified a couple of areas where Democrats and Republicans might come together, pointing to lowering the age of Medicare eligibility, expanding healthcare coverage to include vision, hearing and dental, and making sure that children get coverage, "so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one." "That's a place where we can explore coming together," Jeffries said. "I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare."
